job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 drafting review: loopholes, ambiguities, and enforcement problems

These items cover gaps, inconsistencies, and litigation exposure in the text as provided. Many cut both ways: some could let covered activity continue, and others could sweep in more than the sponsors likely intend. I have tried to describe each problem without judging whether the bill's policy is good. Constitutional points are flagged as risks, not predictions.

## Sec. 2 — Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1) (generally):** "Artificial intelligence," "artificial intelligence model," and "artificial intelligence system" are never defined. Paragraph (A) uses "model" and paragraph (B) uses "system," which invites argument over whether a deployed product (model plus scaffolding, tools, and agents) is the same thing as the trained model.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "single training run":** A developer could structure training as multiple runs, each under 10^26 operations. Examples include staged pretraining, continued pretraining of a checkpoint, fine-tuning, merging, or distillation from a larger model. There is no aggregation or anti-evasion rule.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), counting method:** The bill doesn't say which operations count. Open questions include failed or restarted runs, compute used to generate synthetic training data, reinforcement-learning rollouts, and compute inherited from a base model. Without rulemaking authority, these questions would be litigated case by case.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), static threshold:** The 10^26 figure is fixed in statute with no mechanism to adjust it. Algorithmic efficiency gains could produce highly capable models below the line over time. Meanwhile, the line may already capture frontier-scale models that nobody considers "superintelligent," which creates an overbreadth argument.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary":** The Act never says which Secretary. Sec. 4 references the Department of Commerce, which suggests the Secretary of Commerce, but the text should say so.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), vague standard:** "Substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks" has no defined benchmarks or baseline (average human? expert?). It also lacks any process: no notice, rulemaking, hearing, or appeal. This invites vagueness and nondelegation challenges, as well as Administrative Procedure Act challenges to any determination.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B), timing and fair notice:** Capability can usually only be assessed after a system is trained. A Secretary's determination would therefore attach to conduct (training) that occurred before anyone knew it was covered. That creates a serious fair-notice problem, especially for the criminal penalties in Sec. 5(b).

8. **Sec. 2(2), entity types:** "U.S. person" covers only citizens and "corporations." It omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other entity forms, which are how many AI companies and investment vehicles are organized.

9. **Sec. 2(2), lawful permanent residents:** Green-card holders are excluded. They are bound only while physically in the United States and could do covered work abroad.

10. **Sec. 2(2), "State":** "State" is undefined, so it is unclear whether entities organized under the laws of DC, Puerto Rico, or other territories are covered. Entities chartered under federal law are also not addressed.

11. **Sec. 2(2), foreign subsidiaries:** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary of a U.S. company is not a "U.S. person." It could train abroad unless the parent's involvement is itself treated as "developing." There is no ownership-or-control test.

12. **Sec. 2(3), undefined terms:** "Data center" and "advanced AI chips" are undefined. The chip definition is especially open, given the variety of GPUs, TPUs, custom accelerators, and successive hardware generations.

13. **Sec. 2(3), facility splitting:** The threshold is "more than 50,000" chips per data center. Operators could keep each site at or below 50,000 and train across sites, since distributed training is technically feasible. There is no aggregation rule for commonly owned or networked facilities.

14. **Sec. 2(3) vs. Sec. 2(1)(A), mismatch:** The registry threshold is chip count, while the prohibition threshold is total compute. As chips get faster, a 10^26 run will need fewer chips and can happen in unregistered facilities. Conversely, many registered facilities will never run a covered workload.

## Sec. 3 — Prohibition

15. **Sec. 3(a), undefined verbs:** "Train," "develop," and "deploy" are undefined. "Develop" is especially broad: it could reach research, data preparation, or work on sub-threshold precursors. Combined with criminal penalties, that raises vagueness concerns.

16. **Sec. 3(a), "deploy" and foreign models:** It is unclear whether offering U.S. users access to a covered model trained abroad, by API or by distributing weights, is "deployment in the United States." It is also unclear who would be liable: the foreign developer, the U.S. cloud host, or the end user.

17. **Sec. 3(a), secondary liability:** The bill has no provision on providing compute, chips, financing, or hosting to someone who trains a covered system. Criminal aiding-and-abetting under 18 U.S.C. § 2 may apply, but nothing equivalent exists for civil liability. Possessing or using covered model weights is not addressed.

18. **Sec. 3(a), remote work:** A person "in the United States" contributing remotely to a training run conducted abroad may or may not be covered. The ambiguity could either over-reach (individual engineers) or under-reach (the foreign operator).

19. **Sec. 3(b), scope of the grandfather clause:** Exempt systems are excused from all of subsection (a), not just training. A system whose training "began" before enactment could therefore be trained further, developed, and deployed indefinitely, with no cap on additional compute.

20. **Sec. 3(b), "training began":** What counts as beginning training is undefined. A developer could start a nominal run before enactment and continue scaling it afterward. It is also unclear whether fine-tuned versions, successor checkpoints, or new versions of a grandfathered system inherit the exemption.

21. **Sec. 3(b), pre-enactment race:** Tying the cutoff to enactment gives developers an incentive to start large runs during the period between committee action, floor passage, and signature.

22. **Sec. 3(c), safety-evaluation exemption:** "For the purpose of safety evaluation" is undefined, subjective, and self-declared. The text does not say "solely" or "primarily," and there are no approval, registration, compute limits, or post-evaluation restrictions. Almost any frontier training program could plausibly claim it.

23. **Sec. 3(c), scope of exempted activities:** The exemption covers training and deployment as well as evaluation. Read literally, a system trained or deployed "for safety evaluation" could later be used commercially, since the bill does not address what happens afterward.

## Sec. 4 — Registry

24. **Sec. 4, no penalty for non-compliance:** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing an inaccurate report carries no penalty under this Act. 18 U.S.C. § 1001 (false statements to a federal agency) may cover knowingly false certifications, but not non-filing.

25. **Sec. 4(a), no deadline or process:** The bill sets no registration deadline and no form or contents for registration. It does not define "operator," for example in a colocation facility where the building owner, tenant, and cloud provider may each claim not to be the operator.

26. **Sec. 4(b), vague report content:** "Describing the computing workloads" sets no required detail, such as compute used per run, customer identity, or model purpose. A generic description would technically comply.

27. **Sec. 4, no oversight authority:** Commerce gets no authority to issue regulations, inspect facilities, audit reports, subpoena records, or share information with enforcement agencies. The bill also has no confidentiality protections for trade secrets, which could prompt objections from operators and complicate FOIA handling.

## Sec. 5 — Penalties

28. **Sec. 5(a), no enforcer or procedure:** The bill doesn't say who assesses civil penalties (Commerce administratively? the Attorney General in federal court?) or by what process. Without that, the civil penalty may be difficult to collect. Recent Supreme Court precedent on agency-imposed civil penalties (*SEC v. Jarkesy*, 2024) also makes the choice of forum legally significant.

29. **Sec. 5(a), "each day":** For a discrete act such as "developing" or a multi-month training run, it is unclear what counts as a day of violation. That makes the maximum exposure uncertain.

30. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, timing conflict:** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. The text could be read to reach conduct before the prohibition was in force, raising retroactivity and due process issues. At minimum, it is internally inconsistent.

31. **Sec. 5(a), penalty size:** Reviewers may question whether a $1,000,000 daily cap meaningfully deters companies with very large compute budgets, or whether it should scale with revenue or compute. This is a policy question, but it is likely to come up at markup.

32. **Sec. 5(b), compounded vagueness:** Criminal liability attaches to undefined verbs (item 15), to systems that may be designated only after the fact (item 7), and to a subjective exemption (item 22). Together these strengthen a void-for-vagueness challenge, even with the "willfully" mens rea requirement.

## Sec. 6 — International Agreement

33. **Sec. 6, "seek to negotiate":** The phrase is ambiguous about whether 18 months is the deadline to begin or to conclude negotiations. There is no reporting requirement and no consequence for missing the date. "Equivalent" prohibitions are undefined, and any treaty would need separate Senate advice and consent.

## Sec. 7 — Duration

34. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), conflict:** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress makes a finding. Subsection (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. Read together, the prohibition expires automatically at year 10 even if no safety finding has been made, which undercuts (a).

35. **Sec. 7(a), no report commissioned:** The bill relies on a National Academies report but never requires, funds, or schedules one. Also, because a joint resolution must be signed by the President, (a) adds little beyond Congress's existing power to amend or repeal.

36. **Sec. 7(b), measured from enactment:** The sunset runs from enactment, not the effective date, so the operative prohibition lasts about 9.5 years.

## Sec. 8 — Effective Date

37. **Sec. 8 vs. Sec. 3(b), the 180-day gap:** Training that begins between enactment and the effective date is not grandfathered, but it is also not yet prohibited. On day 181, continuing that training would become unlawful, which raises reliance and takings-style arguments. Developers may also simply concentrate activity in the window.

38. **Sec. 8, no phase-in for Sec. 4:** Registry obligations take effect at the same time as everything else, with no time for Commerce to set up the system. That compounds the missing deadlines noted in item 25.

## Cross-cutting omissions

39. **No rulemaking authority:** Nothing in the Act authorizes regulations. Most of the definitional gaps above therefore cannot be filled administratively and would be resolved in litigation.

40. **No anti-evasion clause:** There is no general prohibition on structuring activities to avoid the thresholds. This affects the run-splitting, facility-splitting, and foreign-subsidiary routes in items 2, 11, and 13.

41. **No severability clause:** Courts generally presume severability, but an express clause would reduce the risk that an invalidated provision, such as Sec. 2(1)(B), brings down related provisions.

42. **No preemption or savings clause:** The bill doesn't address its relationship to state AI laws, leaving room for conflict or duplicative obligations.

43. **Possible First Amendment challenge:** Some courts have treated source code as expressive (e.g., *Bernstein v. U.S. Dep't of Justice*, 9th Cir. 1999). Challengers may argue that restrictions on "developing" or distributing model weights burden speech or research. How strong that argument is remains unsettled.

44. **No whistleblower protections or appropriations:** The bill has no mechanism to surface hidden violations and no funding for Commerce's registry or the Secretary's determinations.

If it's useful for coverage, I can turn this into a reader-facing explainer or a list of questions to put to committee staff and sponsors' offices before Thursday. It would also be worth checking whether any of these points are addressed in pending amendments filed for the markup, which I don't have access to.
